newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Manuel sees South African municipal bond market.
newsitem.headline: Manuel sees South African municipal bond market.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Tuesday he expected a formal municipal bond market to develop in parallel with the existing Infrastructure Finance Corporation (INCA) financing programme.

Analysts said after hearing a presentation by Manuel and Provincial Affairs Minister Mohammed Valli Moosa that the market could be worth tens of billions of rand and might eventually rival the central government finance market.

"We will see the development of a municipal bond market. It will have its own dynamic. The rating system will work there and that will become the key determinant," Manuel told reporters and investors.

South African municipalities are allowed to borrow on the domestic market to fund capital projects, but may not raise funds abroad. Bridging loans to cover operating expenditure must be repaid within 12 months.
The country's municipalities budgeted for capital expenditure of 10.6 billion rand in the fiscal year to June 30.
Chippie Olver, chief director for municipal planning and finance in the ministry of provincial affairs, told Reuters he anticipated a doubling of the existing municipal debt.
"There is a market of 26 billion rand at the moment. That needs to double at the very least," he said.
Olver said the anticipated municipal bond market would operate in parallel with the Infrastructure Finance Corporation, which privately placed its first 500 million rand bond in February.

INCA is a joint venture including First National Bank, the Commonwealth Development Corporation and Southern Life to help fund the country's estimated 171 billion rand requirement to upgrade municipal facilities over the next 10 years.
"We welcome the INCA project, but that is a private initiative. We want to open up as many options as possible for municipalities to fund their capital programmes," he said.

INCA has scheduled bond issues totalling 12 billion rand over the next seven years, but Minister of Provincial Affairs Mohammed Valli Moosa estimated on Tuesday the infrastructure development programme would require loans totalling 80 billion rand over the next decade.
About 97 billion rand would come from foreign aid and grant funds, mainly for housing.

Investec Asset Management managing director Hendrik du Toit said after Tuesday's briefing there would be considerable interest in the market if the government provided more information on which to assess credit risk.

"Once there is certainty, and they're starting to give that kind of certainty, there will be a very big opportunity for municipalities to raise money efficiently and not on a bank loan basis, where the bank has to lock up their assets.
"If you look at the figures here, it could be a larger market than the central government," he told Reuters.
"The concept of a long market for well-developed municipalities is on, it's part of the future. I think that's what you're going to see in the next two years."
Manuel declined to open the books of the government's own Project Liquidity, a programme to assess the viability of municipalities, but said he expected credit rating agencies to enter the market.
About half the country's municipalities, together accounting for over 90 percent of income and expenditure, contribute information to Project Liquidity.

But Manuel said their cooperation was not mandatory, adding: "The quickest way to sink project liquidity is to advise municipalities that this information is now going to become a matter of public record."
Du Toit said he was confident the government understood the need to provide enough information, but said the private sector would have to do the work.
"Professional rating agencies have to go in there. Municipalities will pay and get themselves rated and then they'll get money at the right price," he said.
